initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now. "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), one working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. It starts from this session's pushed branch when it runs in a worktree, else the repository's default branch. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). Must exist; if the user has not trusted it yet the app asks them first. "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one. Self-hosted environments and runner pools need the user's own click and are refused, and so is an environment that cannot run this project's repository.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work: the user follows your progress by it and will never ask for it, so it is part of the task. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

content.description: The step, as a short imperative phrase (≤7 words).

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list. Use on the first call and whenever the plan changes.

advance.description: true: the in_progress step is done and the next pending step starts (the cheap, usual update).

done.description: 1-based numbers of steps just completed (out-of-order updates).

start.description: 1-based number of the step now in progress (with done, for out-of-order updates).

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. {
  "version": "0.9.4",
  "body": "### Added\n- `herdr plugin update` updates plugins installed from GitHub, all at once or by name. Running plugin panes keep working on their old files, and new runs pick up the update without a config reload. Locally linked plugins are left alone. (#4245, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Windows notifications stay in Notification Center. Clicking one jumps to its pane and brings the terminal window forward. (#4773, #4803, thanks @JJLiebig)\n\n### Changed\n- An elevated Windows server now only accepts administrator clients by default. To let normal clients from the same account in, set `[server] allow_unelevated_clients = true` or start the server with `--allow-unelevated-clients`. Permission errors now say how to fix them, and sessions you can't reach show as unavailable instead of stopped. (#4717, #4769, #4777, #4779, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- On Linux and macOS, closing the shell that started Herdr no longer stops the server. Scripts that stopped Herdr with `SIGHUP` should use `herdr server stop` or `SIGTERM`. The server log now says why the server stopped. (#4920, #4965)\n- With mouse capture on, plugins that handle a link get first pick when you click it. Turn capture off to use your terminal's own link shortcuts, like Command-click on macOS. (#4874, #5064, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Antigravity and Grok count as idle once they are back at their prompt, even if their own background tasks or subagents are still running. (#3530, #4735, #4959)\n- Ctrl+Shift+letter reaches plain shells as the Ctrl key, like in Alacritty and WezTerm. Super, Hyper and Meta shortcuts no longer type escape-code junk into apps that can't read them. (#4356, #5017)\n\n### Fixed\n- Restarting a Mac or shutting down Windows keeps your agents' sessions. Herdr saves before the system starts closing apps, so agents come back where they were. (#4414, #5013, #5057, #5092, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Session saves are written to disk before they replace the old file, so a crash or power cut can't leave an unreadable save. (#5150, #5152, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- The server keeps running when the machine runs out of processes or threads, instead of taking every pane down with it. (#3324, #4958)\n- An out-of-range workspace number returns `workspace_not_found` instead of crashing the server. (#5096, #5171)\n- Suspending an agent with Ctrl+Z and bringing it back with `fg` keeps its name and saved conversation. (#1647, #4964)\n- Restoring a session stays responsive when a checkout's Git data is slow or missing. Worktree groups survive checkouts that are temporarily unavailable, and opening the same repository twice no longer nests one workspace inside the other. (#4926, #4736, #4945, #4770, #4772, thanks @minatoaquaMK2 and @JJLiebig)\n- Closing a workspace's only pane asks first, like closing its last tab already does. Turn this off with `ui.confirm_close = false`. (#5143, #5173)\n- Ctrl shortcuts like Ctrl+W work on non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew. Latin layouts and AltGr characters keep their normal meaning. (#1079, #4961)\n- Accent keys and AltGr shortcuts work on Windows. (#4688, #5021, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Shift+Enter and other enhanced keys keep working after the outer terminal resets, for example after VS Code's Reload Window. (#4985, #5088)\n- Quick Escape taps work on macOS with WezTerm's Kitty keyboard mode. (#1266, #5089)\n- Kitty keyboard apps get key releases and F1, F2 and F4 correctly, and Backspace works when the terminal sends Ctrl+H for it. (#4184, #4403, #3244, #5017)\n- Keyboard and terminal color replies no longer leak stray characters into pane input, and a half-finished color reply no longer freezes typing. (#4856, #4025, #5052, #5017, #5087)\n- Fish no longer repeats prompt fragments while you resize a pane. The same problem with zsh and Powerlevel10k is still open, waiting on a Ghostty fix. (#3672, #4977)\n- Apps that ask for pixel mouse coordinates get them, and clicks land in the right place on terminals that only report cells. (#4750, #3675, #5017, #4971)\n- Turning off Kitty graphics makes panes stop advertising image support, so apps fall back to text. (#4978, #4979)\n- Typing shows up faster, especially in PowerShell. (#4884, #5149, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Big sessions use less CPU on busy agents and idle shells, hidden panes use less memory, and Windows panes need fewer threads. (#4506, #5083, #4845, #4847, #4849, #4850, #4873, #5085, #5091, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- New workspaces, tabs and splits start their shell at the right size instead of borrowing another pane's size. (#4419, #4873)\n- Forwarded SSH agents are no longer contacted every second, which could eventually break SSH and Git authentication. (#4931, #4962)\n- Sidebar width, collapsed groups and agent sorting on remote machines survive reconnects. Switching workspaces quickly while changing machines no longer gets canceled. (#4364, #5019, #4536, #5061, thanks @minatoaquaMK2 and @JJLiebig)\n- The sidebar collapse button stays clickable when the agent list has a scrollbar. (#4692, #4734, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n- The welcome screen shows your configured prefix. (#4745, #4747, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Ctrl+[ leaves workspace navigation. (#1431, #2340, thanks @qaz74107410)\n- Keybindings that use `+` survive config reloads, and `/` opens Go To search on layouts where it needs Shift. (#4960, #4963, #4983, #5090, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n- Pasting from WezTerm on Windows into remote panes no longer types encoded key data. Copying no longer adds duplicate clipboard history entries, and closing a pane no longer hangs on a pending Enter. (#4725, #4730, #4709, #4872, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Windows shells started through Scoop or 32-bit wrappers keep their working directory in new tabs and after restarts. (#4472, #4749, #5062, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Windows ARM64 machines can be used as remote hosts through the x64 build, on a best-effort basis. (#4752)\n- Codex reports finished turns through its integration when started with `--no-daemon`, its startup update screen shows as blocked, and Codex and Pi status is recognized in more cases. (#4507, #4811, #4756, #5174, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Antigravity permission, question and workspace-trust dialogs show as blocked, and its thinking spinner shows as working. (#3871, #3419, #3530, #4959)\n- Hermes started through its Python installer is recognized, and installing or removing its integration keeps your YAML plugin list intact. (#4910, #4909, #4911, #4984, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n- On macOS, `pane run` and `agent start` refuse commands too long for a shell that is still starting, instead of silently cutting them off. (#4950, #4988, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n\n### Removed\n- The experimental `HERDR_WINDOWS_INPUT_BACKEND=crossterm` setting is gone. Windows always uses its native console input. (#5017)",
  "show_on_startup": true

{
  "version": "0.9.4",
  "body": "### Added\n- `herdr plugin update` updates plugins installed from GitHub, all at once or by name. Running plugin panes keep working on their old files, and new runs pick up the update without a config reload. Locally linked plugins are left alone. (#4245, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Windows notifications stay in Notification Center. Clicking one jumps to its pane and brings the terminal window forward. (#4773, #4803, thanks @JJLiebig)\n\n### Changed\n- An elevated Windows server now only accepts administrator clients by default. To let normal clients from the same account in, set `[server] allow_unelevated_clients = true` or start the server with `--allow-unelevated-clients`. Permission errors now say how to fix them, and sessions you can't reach show as unavailable instead of stopped. (#4717, #4769, #4777, #4779, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- On Linux and macOS, closing the shell that started Herdr no longer stops the server. Scripts that stopped Herdr with `SIGHUP` should use `herdr server stop` or `SIGTERM`. The server log now says why the server stopped. (#4920, #4965)\n- With mouse capture on, plugins that handle a link get first pick when you click it. Turn capture off to use your terminal's own link shortcuts, like Command-click on macOS. (#4874, #5064, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Antigravity and Grok count as idle once they are back at their prompt, even if their own background tasks or subagents are still running. (#3530, #4735, #4959)\n- Ctrl+Shift+letter reaches plain shells as the Ctrl key, like in Alacritty and WezTerm. Super, Hyper and Meta shortcuts no longer type escape-code junk into apps that can't read them. (#4356, #5017)\n\n### Fixed\n- Restarting a Mac or shutting down Windows keeps your agents' sessions. Herdr saves before the system starts closing apps, so agents come back where they were. (#4414, #5013, #5057, #5092, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Session saves are written to disk before they replace the old file, so a crash or power cut can't leave an unreadable save. (#5150, #5152, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- The server keeps running when the machine runs out of processes or threads, instead of taking every pane down with it. (#3324, #4958)\n- An out-of-range workspace number returns `workspace_not_found` instead of crashing the server. (#5096, #5171)\n- Suspending an agent with Ctrl+Z and bringing it back with `fg` keeps its name and saved conversation. (#1647, #4964)\n- Restoring a session stays responsive when a checkout's Git data is slow or missing. Worktree groups survive checkouts that are temporarily unavailable, and opening the same repository twice no longer nests one workspace inside the other. (#4926, #4736, #4945, #4770, #4772, thanks @minatoaquaMK2 and @JJLiebig)\n- Closing a workspace's only pane asks first, like closing its last tab already does. Turn this off with `ui.confirm_close = false`. (#5143, #5173)\n- Ctrl shortcuts like Ctrl+W work on non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew. Latin layouts and AltGr characters keep their normal meaning. (#1079, #4961)\n- Accent keys and AltGr shortcuts work on Windows. (#4688, #5021, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Shift+Enter and other enhanced keys keep working after the outer terminal resets, for example after VS Code's Reload Window. (#4985, #5088)\n- Quick Escape taps work on macOS with WezTerm's Kitty keyboard mode. (#1266, #5089)\n- Kitty keyboard apps get key releases and F1, F2 and F4 correctly, and Backspace works when the terminal sends Ctrl+H for it. (#4184, #4403, #3244, #5017)\n- Keyboard and terminal color replies no longer leak stray characters into pane input, and a half-finished color reply no longer freezes typing. (#4856, #4025, #5052, #5017, #5087)\n- Fish no longer repeats prompt fragments while you resize a pane. The same problem with zsh and Powerlevel10k is still open, waiting on a Ghostty fix. (#3672, #4977)\n- Apps that ask for pixel mouse coordinates get them, and clicks land in the right place on terminals that only report cells. (#4750, #3675, #5017, #4971)\n- Turning off Kitty graphics makes panes stop advertising image support, so apps fall back to text. (#4978, #4979)\n- Typing shows up faster, especially in PowerShell. (#4884, #5149, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Big sessions use less CPU on busy agents and idle shells, hidden panes use less memory, and Windows panes need fewer threads. (#4506, #5083, #4845, #4847, #4849, #4850, #4873, #5085, #5091, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- New workspaces, tabs and splits start their shell at the right size instead of borrowing another pane's size. (#4419, #4873)\n- Forwarded SSH agents are no longer contacted every second, which could eventually break SSH and Git authentication. (#4931, #4962)\n- Sidebar width, collapsed groups and agent sorting on remote machines survive reconnects. Switching workspaces quickly while changing machines no longer gets canceled. (#4364, #5019, #4536, #5061, thanks @minatoaquaMK2 and @JJLiebig)\n- The sidebar collapse button stays clickable when the agent list has a scrollbar. (#4692, #4734, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n- The welcome screen shows your configured prefix. (#4745, #4747, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Ctrl+[ leaves workspace navigation. (#1431, #2340, thanks @qaz74107410)\n- Keybindings that use `+` survive config reloads, and `/` opens Go To search on layouts where it needs Shift. (#4960, #4963, #4983, #5090, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n- Pasting from WezTerm on Windows into remote panes no longer types encoded key data. Copying no longer adds duplicate clipboard history entries, and closing a pane no longer hangs on a pending Enter. (#4725, #4730, #4709, #4872, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Windows shells started through Scoop or 32-bit wrappers keep their working directory in new tabs and after restarts. (#4472, #4749, #5062, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Windows ARM64 machines can be used as remote hosts through the x64 build, on a best-effort basis. (#4752)\n- Codex reports finished turns through its integration when started with `--no-daemon`, its startup update screen shows as blocked, and Codex and Pi status is recognized in more cases. (#4507, #4811, #4756, #5174, thanks @JJLiebig)\n- Antigravity permission, question and workspace-trust dialogs show as blocked, and its thinking spinner shows as working. (#3871, #3419, #3530, #4959)\n- Hermes started through its Python installer is recognized, and installing or removing its integration keeps your YAML plugin list intact. (#4910, #4909, #4911, #4984, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n- On macOS, `pane run` and `agent start` refuse commands too long for a shell that is still starting, instead of silently cutting them off. (#4950, #4988, thanks @minatoaquaMK2)\n\n### Removed\n- The experimental `HERDR_WINDOWS_INPUT_BACKEND=crossterm` setting is gone. Windows always uses its native console input. (#5017)",

content.content:
## Theme

Choose a built-in theme:

```toml
[theme]
name = "catppuccin"
```

Search `theme.name` in the [Config reference](/docs/config-reference/) for every built-in theme. Use `terminal` when you want Herdr UI colors to follow your host terminal's ANSI palette.

On Unix, Herdr also re-reads the host terminal's colors when redrawing after a resize or `SIGWINCH`. If your theme switcher changes terminal colors through OSC without a light/dark notification, send `kill -WINCH <client-pid>` after applying the new palette. Target the attached Herdr client, not the server; existing panes stay running. Direct `herdr terminal attach` sessions leave palette queries to the attached application.

To let Herdr switch its own UI theme when the host terminal reports a light/dark appearance change, enable theme auto-switching:

```toml
[theme]
name = "catppuccin"
auto_switch = true
light_name = "catppuccin-latte"
dark_name = "catppuccin"
```

`auto_switch` defaults to `false`, so existing theme configs keep manual behavior. If `light_name` or `dark_name` is omitted, Herdr uses the matching built-in sibling for the configured `name` when one exists, such as `tokyo-night`/`tokyo-night-day` or `gruvbox`/`gruvbox-light`. Manual theme selection in Settings disables `auto_switch`.

You can override individual colors:

```toml
[theme.custom]
sidebar_bg = "#181825"
active_row_bg = "#1e1e2e"
selection_bg = "#313244"
panel_bg = "reset"
accent = "#a6e3a1"
green = "#a6e3a1"
blue = "#89b4fa"
red = "#f38ba8"
yellow = "#f9e2af"
```

`sidebar_bg` optionally gives the desktop sidebar its own background. When omitted, the sidebar keeps the host terminal background. `active_row_bg` changes the active Space and focused Agent row background without affecting separators or scrollbar tracks. `selection_bg` changes the Navigate-mode cursor row background in the sidebar.

Color values accept hex, named colors, `rgb(r,g,b)`, or reset aliases like `reset`, `default`, `none`, and `transparent`.

When `auto_switch` is enabled, optional light and dark subtables layer on top of the shared custom colors:

```toml
[theme.custom]
accent = "#89b4fa"

[theme.custom.light]
panel_bg = "#eff1f5"
text = "#4c4f69"

[theme.custom.dark]
panel_bg = "#1e1e2e"
text = "#cdd6f4"
```

The active palette is applied in this order: built-in theme, `[theme.custom]`, then `[theme.custom.light]` or `[theme.custom.dark]`. Omitting the mode subtables preserves the existing shared override behavior.

# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-voice)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - **Fullscreen / expand buttons**: there is no fullscreen. Never call any element's `requestFullscreen()`, never call `document.exitFullscreen()`, and never key state on `document.fullscreenElement` (the API is dead inside the widget iframe and `fullscreenElement` stays null forever, so a label or branch keyed on it is permanently stuck), never call display-mode host APIs, and never fake fullscreen by restyling your container to viewport size — all of these produce dead or broken controls on at least one platform. If the user asks for a fullscreen or expand button, implement an expanded-layout toggle instead: a synchronous CSS class flip on in-flow content with explicit px sizes (taller chart, roomier controls), updating the button label in the same handler — no async, no awaits, symmetric enter/exit. Mutate the existing elements' classes and text; never rebuild the control's DOM with innerHTML (replacement silently drops event listeners and leaves a dead button). The host resizes to fit your content automatically. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--radius)` for controls, `12px` for cards. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - **Validate input in interactive widgets.** Any widget that collects user input before acting on it (quiz answers, text boxes, form fields) must check that input in its submit handler: if a required field is empty or invalid, show a clear inline error next to the control (13px `color: var(--text-danger)` text, e.g. "Enter an answer first") and stop — do not advance to the next step, reveal the answer, or otherwise proceed until the input is valid. Tokens tell you _what_ you can use; the [Rules](../CLAUDE.md#rules) tell you _how_ to apply them. These principles tell you _why_. ## Claude-native cds is designed to be authored _by_ Claude as much as _for_ Claude's products. The `CLAUDE.md` you're reading is the system prompt; component docs are structured for retrieval; utilities are named so a model can guess them; the GenerateDemo page proves the loop works. A design system an LLM can use fluently is one humans can use fluently too. ## Clay is Claude's color `brand` (clay) is reserved for what Claude does — send, generate, the spark mark. User-driven primary actions take the neutral `accent` blue; everything else stays gray. Holding clay back to a single role is what lets it carry meaning instead of becoming wallpaper. ## Serif is Claude's voice Claude's responses render in serif; the surrounding chrome stays sans. Typography signals who's speaking before a word is read. cds ships `--font-voice` (the `font-voice` utility) for response surfaces. ## Density adapts to the surface Console, claude.ai and antfarm share the same components — `compact` for dev tools and power users, `comfortable` for consumer apps. Density is one switch on `CdsRoot`, not a per-component prop, so a product can change its feel without forking a single component. ## Built to be composed, not overridden Every component takes `className` for placement and behavior, every token is a public CSS var, and compound parts (`.Root`, `.Item`, `.Trigger`) sit under the porcelain helpers so you can recombine them. The system expects you to compose _with_ it — wrap it, arrange it, fill its slots, build new things from its tokens — not restyle it from outside or fork it. When props and parts can't reach what you need, the system is missing something: the fix goes into cds (see the [`className` rule](../CLAUDE.md#classname-rule)), not around it. ## Restraint over options One accent per view, one elevation step, t-shirt sizes instead of 0–12 scales. Fewer decisions at the call site means fewer ways for two screens to drift apart — consistency comes from removing knobs, not policing them. ## CDS tokens Every visual decision in `@ant/cds` resolves to a `--*` CSS custom property. The TypeScript source of truth lives under `packages/cds/tokens/`; `yarn gen:tokens` emits the shipped CSS at [`src/generated/tokens.css`](../src/generated/tokens.css). The tints are solved against the stock `surface-1`, so a theme that overrides `--surface-*` should override `--bg-tint-*` in the same block if it needs the exact stops, and `--bg-tint-*-opaque` with them: inside a fill scope the inline pin reads the opaque token, not the tint. #### `git-*` roles Diff and PR/CR-state colors — `added`, `removed`, `modified`, `conflicting`, `merged`, `closed`, `draft`, plus `opened`/`queued` as aliases of `added`/`modified`. Each carries the full `text` / `fill{,-hover}` / `bg` / `border` / `on` suite. Values are hues matching the palette claude.ai's diff UI was built on (not CDS ramp stops), so adopting them there is a pure rename; `fill` light is the hue darkened just enough for white `on-git-*` to pass AA. ### Background vs. fill Both are backgrounds; the split is saturation, and therefore which foreground token pairs on top. `bg-{role}` is the pale tint (hue-100 light / hue-800 dark) for passive status surfaces — Banner, chip; Badge paints its translucent twin `bg-tint-{hue}`. Light enough that `text-{role}` (hue-600) reads against it: a danger banner is `bg-danger` + `text-danger`. `fill-{role}` is the saturated solid (hue-450) for interactive controls — button, checkbox, toggle. Too dark for `text-{role}`, so it pairs with `on-{role}` (gray-0 / gray-900) instead; the 450 stop is chosen for WCAG contrast against `on-*`. | | Background | Foreground | Example | | ----- | ------------- | ------------- | ------------- | | Tint | `bg-{role}` | `text-{role}` | Banner, Toast | | Solid | `fill-{role}` | `on-{role}` | Button | The token name encodes the pairing: use `bg-*` when the hue is ambient context behind body text; `fill-*` when the hue _is_ the control surface. ### Purpose tokens | Token | Value (light) | Use case | | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | | `--text-primary` | `neutral-900` | Body text | | `--text-secondary` | `neutral-600` | Supporting text | | `--text-muted` | `neutral-400` | Placeholder, captions | | `--text-disabled` | `alpha-4` | Disabled labels | | `--border` | `alpha-2` | Default 1px hairline | | `--border-strong` | `alpha-3` | Emphasized divider | | `--border-stronger` | `neutral-900 / 40%` | Heavy divider | | `--fill-primary` | `neutral-900` | Primary button bg | | `--fill-primary-hover` | `neutral-750` | | | `--fill-secondary` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.1)` | Secondary button bg | | `--fill-secondary-hover` | `alpha-1` | | | `--fill-secondary-ring` | `border` (light) / transparent (dark) | Secondary button ring | | `--fill-field` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.5)` (light) / `alpha-1` (dark) | Field control bg (TextInput, TextArea, Combobox) | | `--fill-field-ring` | `border` (light + dark) | Field control resting ring | | `--fill-ghost-hover` | `alpha-1` (light) / 7.5% white (dark half-step) | Ghost button / row hover bg | | `--fill-ghost-selected` | `alpha-2` (light) / 15% white (dark half-step) | Ghost row / nav item selected bg | | `--fill-control` | `alpha-2` | Avatar fallback bg | | `--fill-control-hover` | `alpha-3` | | | `--fill-disabled` | `alpha-1` | Disabled control bg | | `--on-primary` | `neutral-0` | Text on `fill-primary` | | `--on-accent` | `gray-0` | Text on `accent` | | `--on-brand` | `#ffffff` | Text on `brand` | | `--on-danger` | `gray-0` | Text on `danger` | | `--on-success` | `gray-900` | Text on `success` | | `--on-warning` | `gray-900` | Text on `warning` | | `--on-pro` | `gray-0` | Text on `pro` | | `--focus-shadow` | `0 0 0 1px accent, 0 0 6px 1px bg-accent` | `focus-visible` ring | | `--shadow-sm` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Low elevation | | `--shadow-md` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Card / panel | | `--shadow-lg` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Dialog / sheet | | `--shadow-popover` | `0 8px 24px /12%, 0 2px 6px /8%` | Menu, dropdown popups | | `--surface-popover` | `surface-3` | Named alias | | `--surface-panel` | `surface-2` | Named alias | `--shadow-sm/md/lg` are two-layer composites (contact + diffused drop) driven by `--shadow-color`, which deepens to `black/24%` in dark mode. `--shadow-popover` is a fixed two-layer literal tuned for floating menus. --- ## CDS content How to write the words that go inside cds components. Tokens decide how the UI _looks_; this decides how it _sounds_. The voice is **intelligent, warm, unvarnished, and collaborative** — your smartest friend explaining something in plain terms. Friendly lives in the copy, not in extra chrome. ## Mechanics - **Sentence case everywhere.** Buttons, headings, tabs, labels, menu items. "Save changes", not "Save Changes". Title Case is for proper nouns only (Claude, Opus, Anthropic Console). - **No terminal punctuation on labels and headings.** Helper text, descriptions, and empty-state body copy _do_ end with a period. - **Use contractions.** "Can't", "you'll", "it's". Conversational, not stiff. - **Active voice, verb first.** "Delete project", not "Project deletion". - **Ellipsis = in progress only.** "Claude is thinking…". Not for trailing off, not for menu suffixes. - **No ampersands.** Spell out "and". - **Serial comma.** "Chats, projects, and artifacts." ## Pronouns UI speaks as the product, not as Claude and not as the user. | Context | Use | Example | | ---------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | User's things | **your** | "Your projects" — never "My projects" | | Confirmations | none / past tense | "Saved", "Got it" — never "I saved it" | | Errors | **you / your** | "Your session expired" — never "I couldn't…" | | Claude (in chat) | **I** | Reserved for the chat surface; system UI never says "I" | ## Words to avoid | Skip | Why | Instead | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------- | | "successfully" | The success toast _is_ the success | "File uploaded" | | "please" | UI isn't asking a favor | "Enter a name" | | "Click here" / "Tap to…" | Link text should name the destination | "Read the docs" | | "!" on system copy | Reads as shouty | "Settings saved" | | "leverage", "seamless", "unlock", "empower" | Corporate filler | Say what it does | | "simply", "just", "easy" | Presumes — and condescends | Cut it | ## Patterns **Buttons / CTAs** — verb first, 1–3 words, sentence case, no punctuation. "Create project", "Upgrade to Pro". Not "OK", "Submit", or "Click to continue". **Errors** — say what happened, then what to do. One sentence, no "Error:" prefix, no first person. "That name's already taken. Try another." Never surface raw exception strings. **Empty states** — an invitation, not an apology. Headline names the space ("Start your first project"), one-line body explains it, CTA is a verb ("Create project"). Skip "Nothing here yet." **Placeholders** — a real example of valid input ("name@company.com", "Summarize this document"). No "e.g." prefix, don't repeat the field label. **Links** — describe where they go ("Learn more", "View pricing"). Keep them at the end of the sentence; punctuation sits outside the link. ## Do / Don't | Do | Don't | | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | "File uploaded" | "Your file was uploaded successfully!" | | "Enter a workspace name" | "Please enter a workspace name." | | "Couldn't connect to Slack. Retry" | "Error: I was unable to connect." | | "Your projects" | "My projects" | | "Create project" | "Click Here To Get Started" | | "Connect Slack" | "Add the Slack Connector" | Do not overthink. Try to keep thinking below 500 tokens. If the visual is complex and requires more reasoning effort, consider creating an artifact instead.
